title: A Virtually Unlimited Line of Credit, Funded by the Customers: What the SEC Alleged About FTX and Alameda

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The equity raise is the figure the Commission puts first: more than $1.8 billion from investors "who bought an equity stake in FTX believing that FTX had appropriate controls and risk management measures". The customer float is the larger pool, and the complaint alleges it was moving out from the beginning: "from the start, Bankman-Fried improperly diverted customer assets to his privately-held crypto hedge fund".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise alleged is an exemption written into the platform itself. Investors were told "that FTX had top-notch, sophisticated automated risk measures in place to protect customer assets, that those assets were safe and secure, and that Alameda was just another platform customer with no special privileges." The complaint alleges the opposite was true: Alameda was exempted from the risk mitigation measures and given "significant special treatment on the FTX platform, including a virtually unlimited 'line of credit' funded by the platform's customers."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was a public persona maintained while the diversion ran. "Throughout this period, Bankman-Fried portrayed himself as a responsible leader of the crypto community. He touted the importance of regulation and accountability. He told the public, including investors, that FTX was both innovative and responsible." The complaint alleges the customer funds went to "undisclosed venture investments, lavish real estate purchases, and large political donations" — the undisclosed venture book and the political giving both being, in effect, reputational spend financed from the float.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was time. When crypto prices fell in May 2022 and Alameda's lenders called their loans, the complaint alleges Bankman-Fried "directed FTX to divert billions more in customer assets to Alameda to ensure that Alameda maintained its lending relationships, and that money could continue to flow in from lenders and other investors." Through that summer he is alleged to have directed hundreds of millions more, used for further venture investments and for "loans" to himself and other executives.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: There is no commission and no liability shield in this one; it ended in a filing. FTX, Alameda "and their tangled web of affiliated entities filed for bankruptcy on November 11, 2022", and the Commission sued a month later, charging violations of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5. A complaint is an accusation: this dossier records it as one.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: An offshore crypto exchange holding customer assets in commingled form, with an affiliated proprietary trading firm on the other side of the platform and no regulator examining either.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-FTX enforcement posture and custody debate; and, as precedent, the Commission's use of the ordinary anti-fraud provisions — Section 17(a), Section 10(b), Rule 10b-5 — against the operator of a crypto platform.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Customer deposits funded the affiliate's positions; the affiliate's apparent strength supported the platform's reputation; the reputation attracted the next round of deposits and the next equity raise, which were needed because the earlier deposits were no longer there.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That FTX was a sound exchange brought down by a bank run — bad luck, a liquidity crunch, a crypto winter — or alternatively that the whole thing was obvious to anyone paying attention and the investors were simply greedy.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The run account is not what the Commission alleges. Its complaint puts the diversion of customer assets "from the start", years before November 2022, and describes the May 2022 price fall as the moment an existing hole became unservable rather than its cause. The blame-the-investors account fails on the complaint's own description of what they were told: that FTX had "top-notch, sophisticated automated risk measures", that customer assets were "safe and secure", and that Alameda was "just another platform customer with no special privileges" — statements the Commission alleges were false, concealing an exemption from the risk engine and a virtually unlimited line of credit funded by customers. What this dossier does not do is treat any of that as established: it is a civil complaint, and the criminal case that followed was not sourced here, so no verdict is asserted.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A complaint filed by the Securities and Exchange Commission in the Southern District of New York on 13 December 2022, alleging a scheme running from at least May 2019 to November 2022; more than $1.8 billion raised from equity investors; customer assets diverted to Alameda Research from the start and used for undisclosed venture investments, real estate and political donations; Alameda exempted from the platform's risk measures and given a virtually unlimited line of credit funded by customers; billions more diverted after May 2022 to keep Alameda's lenders in place; and charges under Section 17(a) of the Securities Act and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 of the Exchange Act. The bankruptcy filing of 11 November 2022 is recorded in the same document. Everything else about this matter — including anything decided in a courtroom afterwards — is outside what was read for this dossier.

citations.title: Securities and Exchange Commission v. Samuel Bankman-Fried, Complaint, No. 1:22-cv-10501 (S.D.N.Y., filed 13 December 2022)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from sec.gov and read as extracted text. (sec.gov refuses a generic browser user-agent and serves the file to a request declaring an identity and contact address, so automated link checks report sec.gov URLs as blocked.) EVERYTHING BELOW IS AN ALLEGATION IN A CIVIL COMPLAINT, NOT A FINDING. The Summary alleges: "From at least May 2019 through November 2022, Bankman-Fried engaged in a scheme to defraud equity investors in FTX Trading Ltd. ('FTX'), the crypto asset trading platform of which he was CEO and co-founder, at the same time that he was also defrauding the platform's customers. Bankman-Fried raised more than $1.8 billion from investors, including U.S. investors, who bought an equity stake in FTX believing that FTX had appropriate controls and risk management measures. Unbeknownst to those investors (and to FTX's trading customers), Bankman-Fried was orchestrating a massive, years-long fraud, diverting billions of dollars of the trading platform's customer funds for his own personal benefit and to help grow his crypto empire." On the public posture: "Throughout this period, Bankman-Fried portrayed himself as a responsible leader of the crypto community. He touted the importance of regulation and accountability." On the mechanism alleged: "from the start, Bankman-Fried improperly diverted customer assets to his privately-held crypto hedge fund, Alameda Research LLC ('Alameda'), and then used those customer funds to make undisclosed venture investments, lavish real estate purchases, and large political donations." On what investors were told: "He told investors and prospective investors that FTX had top-notch, sophisticated automated risk measures in place to protect customer assets, that those assets were safe and secure, and that Alameda was just another platform customer with no special privileges. These statements were false and misleading. In truth, Bankman-Fried had exempted Alameda from the risk mitigation measures and had provided Alameda with significant special treatment on the FTX platform, including a virtually unlimited 'line of credit' funded by the platform's customers." On the collapse: when crypto prices fell in May 2022 and Alameda's lenders demanded repayment, "Bankman-Fried directed FTX to divert billions more in customer assets to Alameda"; through the summer of 2022 he "directed hundreds of millions more in FTX customer funds to Alameda, which he then used for additional venture investments and for 'loans' to himself and other FTX executives"; and the scheme ended when "FTX, Alameda, and their tangled web of affiliated entities filed for bankruptcy on November 11, 2022." The complaint charges violations of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5. The criminal proceedings in the Southern District of New York were NOT sourced for this dossier — justice.gov serves a not-found page for the press releases and nothing from it was read — so no verdict or sentence is asserted anywhere in it.
